title: Semi-supervised learning extension
description: Features from the discriminator or inference net could improve performance of classifiers when limited labeled data is available.
canonical_description: use discriminator features for semi-supervised learning

evidence.anchor: features from the discriminator or inference net could improve performance
evidence.quote: \item { Semi-supervised learning}: features from the discriminator or inference net could improve performance

verdict.reasoning: The gap — that discriminator features can improve classifiers under limited labeled data — is directly validated by two papers. DiscrimNet (Paper 3) uses discriminator features from a DCGAN as unsupervised pre-training for video action recognition, demonstrating that these features outperform random initialization on small labeled sets. The IPM-based GAN study (Paper 4) shows how the K+1 critic formulation, which shares features between the discriminator and a classifier, significantly improves SSL performance across CIFAR-10 and SVHN. These two direct_solution papers span different domains (video vs. image) and GAN families (DCGAN vs. IPM-GANs), confirming the general claim. The partial_solution papers (SGAN, Bad GAN, SR-GAN) provide corroborating evidence: SGAN and Bad GAN use discriminator-as-classifier weight-sharing (a distinct but related mechanism), and SR-GAN applies feature-contrasting to regression, all showing that GAN components aid SSL. The gap is solved because the core claim has been demonstrated concretely; the open specifics noted in individual assessments (domain scope, GAN type) do not undermine the general finding.

paper.title: Semi-Supervised Learning with Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: We extend Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to the semi-supervised context by forcing the discriminator network to output class labels. We train a generative model G and a discriminator D on a dataset with inputs belonging to one of N classes. At training time, D is made to predict which of N+1 classes the input belongs to, where an extra class is added to correspond to the outputs of G. We show that this method can be used to create a more data-efficient classifier and that it allows for generating higher quality samples than a regular GAN.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes the Semi-Supervised GAN (SGAN), which modifies the GAN discriminator to output N+1 classes (N real classes + 1 fake class), making the discriminator itself serve as a classifier through shared weights. This allows simultaneous training of a generative model and a classifier, improving classification performance on limited labeled data (e.g., MNIST with restricted training sets). The approach is related to the gap's goal of using GAN components for semi-supervised learning, but uses weight-sharing rather than extracting discriminator features as inputs to a separate classifier.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap specifically asks about using "features from the discriminator or inference net" as inputs to improve a classifier. The SGAN instead makes the discriminator and classifier share weights (the same network outputs both class labels and real/fake decisions), rather than extracting intermediate features from the discriminator to feed into a separate classifier network. The paper explicitly contrasts its approach with the feature-reuse approach of Radford et al. (DCGAN), arguing against it. Therefore, the specific mechanism of using discriminator features (intermediate representations) to augment a separate classifier remains open — the paper solves a related but distinct approach to semi-supervised learning with GANs.
evidence_snippets: In Radford et al. \yrcite{DCGAN}, the features learned by D are reused in classifiers.
If we simply use the learned representations of D after the fact to augment C, we don't take advantage of this.
D could have N+1 output units corresponding to [CLASS-1, CLASS-2, \dots CLASS-N, FAKE]. In this case, D can also act as C.

paper.title: Good Semi-supervised Learning that Requires a Bad GAN
paper.abstract: Semi-supervised learning methods based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) obtained strong empirical results, but it is not clear 1) how the discriminator benefits from joint training with a generator, and 2) why good semi-supervised classification performance and a good generator cannot be obtained at the same time. Theoretically, we show that given the discriminator objective, good semisupervised learning indeed requires a bad generator, and propose the definition of a preferred generator. Empirically, we derive a novel formulation based on our analysis that substantially improves over feature matching GANs, obtaining state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmark datasets.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper theoretically and empirically analyzes GAN-based semi-supervised learning, showing that a "bad" (complement) generator is needed for good SSL performance rather than a perfect generator. It proposes a novel training objective that addresses drawbacks of feature matching GANs, achieving state-of-the-art SSL results on MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10. The discriminator in this framework doubles as the classifier (using a K+1 class output), so its features f(x) are inherently used for classification. However, the paper's focus is on the generator being complementary and the training dynamics, not on explicitly extracting or leveraging discriminator features to improve a separate classifier.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap asks about using "features from the discriminator or inference net" to improve classifiers under limited labeled data. This paper does not specifically investigate or demonstrate that discriminator features (e.g., from intermediate layers) can be extracted and used to improve a separate classifier. Instead, the discriminator itself IS the classifier (K+1 class softmax), so feature usage is inherent and not a separate mechanism. The paper does not compare against baselines that use discriminator features as input to a separate classifier, nor does it ablate whether the features themselves (as opposed to the GAN training objective) drive the improvement. The gap of explicitly leveraging discriminator features as a general technique for semi-supervised learning remains open.
evidence_snippets: Semi-supervised learning methods based on generative adversarial networks (GANs) obtained strong empirical results, but it is not clear 1) how the discriminator benefits from joint training with a generator, and 2) why good semi-supervised classification performance and a good generator cannot be obtained at the same time.

Let f(x) be a nonlinear vector-valued function, and w_k be the weight vector for class k. As a standard setting in previous work, the discriminator D is defined as P_D(k | x) = exp(w_k^T f(x)) / sum_{k'=1}^{K+1} exp(w_{k'}^T f(x)).

In this work, we present a semi-supervised learning framework that uses generated data to boost task performance. Under this framework, we characterize the properties of various generators and theoretically prove that a complementary (i.e. bad) generator improves generalization.

paper.title: DiscrimNet: Semi-Supervised Action Recognition from Videos using Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: We propose an action recognition framework using Gen- erative Adversarial Networks. Our model involves train- ing a deep convolutional generative adversarial network (DCGAN) using a large video activity dataset without la- bel information. Then we use the trained discriminator from the GAN model as an unsupervised pre-training step and fine-tune the trained discriminator model on a labeled dataset to recognize human activities. We determine good network architectural and hyperparameter settings for us- ing the discriminator from DCGAN as a trained model to learn useful representations for action recognition. Our semi-supervised framework using only appearance infor- mation achieves superior or comparable performance to the current state-of-the-art semi-supervised action recog- nition methods on two challenging video activity datasets: UCF101 and HMDB51.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes using the discriminator network from a DCGAN as an unsupervised pre-training step for action recognition in videos. The discriminator is trained on unlabeled video frames (UCF101, HMDB51, or ImageNet) using adversarial training, then fine-tuned on labeled video action datasets. The authors systematically study architectural choices, hyperparameters, and show that GAN-based initialization significantly outperforms random initialization and achieves competitive or superior results compared to other semi-supervised action recognition methods. This directly demonstrates that features learned by the discriminator during GAN training can improve classifier performance when limited labeled data is available.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the core idea of the gap — using discriminator features for semi-supervised learning — for the specific domain of video action recognition. However, it does not explore: (1) using features from the generator or inference net (only the discriminator), (2) the more advanced semi-supervised GAN techniques that modify the discriminator to output multiple classes (like Salimans et al.'s improved GAN or feature matching), (3) settings where labeled data is extremely scarce (e.g., 1-10 labels per class), and (4) the approach is limited to appearance-based features from single video frames rather than leveraging temporal information. The paper also does not compare against standard semi-supervised baselines that use the same labeled data amounts (e.g., varying percentages of labels).
evidence_snippets: We propose to use the discriminator trained to only differentiate between a real and generated sample for learning a feature representation of actions in videos.

We use the GAN setup to train a discriminator network and use the learned representation of discriminator as ``initialized weight.'' Then fine-tune that discriminator on labeled video dataset such as UCF101

Our unsupervised pre-training step avoids any manual feature engineering, video frame encoding, searching for the best video frame sampling technique and results in an action recognition performance competitive to the state-of-the-art using only appearance information.

paper.title: Semi-Supervised Learning with IPM-based GANs: an Empirical Study
paper.abstract: We present an empirical investigation of a recent class of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) using Integral Probability Metrics (IPM) and their performance for semi-supervised learning. IPM-based GANs like Wasserstein GAN, Fisher GAN and Sobolev GAN have desirable properties in terms of theoretical understanding, training stability, and a meaningful loss. In this work we investigate how the design of the critic (or discriminator) influences the performance in semi-supervised learning. We distill three key take-aways which are important for good SSL performance: (1) the K+1 formulation, (2) avoiding batch normalization in the critic and (3) avoiding gradient penalty constraints on the classification layer.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper empirically investigates how IPM-based GANs (Wasserstein, Fisher, Sobolev GANs) can be used for semi-supervised learning by sharing features between the critic/discriminator and a classifier via the $K+1$ formulation. It shows that the $K+1$ critic formulation, where the "real" direction uses the classifier's $K$ class directions and competes with a $K+1$th "fake" direction, significantly improves SSL performance over plain critic formulations. The paper provides concrete guidelines: (1) the $K+1$ formulation is superior, (2) batch normalization should be avoided in the critic, and (3) gradient penalty constraints should act only on the fake direction $f_-$, not on the full critic including the classifier.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap for IPM-based GANs (Fisher, Sobolev, WGAN) with the $K+1$ formulation. However, the gap is broader than what this single paper covers: it does not investigate using discriminator features for SSL in non-IPM-based GANs beyond what was already known (e.g., the original JSD-based GANs), nor does it explore alternative ways of leveraging discriminator features (e.g., using intermediate layer features as fixed representations, feature matching, or distillation approaches). The paper is also limited to CIFAR-10 and SVHN datasets with specific CNN architectures.
evidence_snippets: We will investigate the ``$K+1$ parametrization" of the critic ... Intuitively this critic uses the $K$ class directions of the classifier $S_y$ to define the ``real'' direction, which competes with another $K+1$\textsuperscript{th} direction $v$ that indicates fake samples.
We see that in the two succesful IPMs (Fisher and Fisher+Sobolev), the $K+1$ formulations give a strong gain over the plain formulation.

Our main conclusions are (1) the $K+1$ formulation works, (2) batch normalization should be avoided, also in Fisher GAN, and (3) gradient penalty constraints should act on $f_-$ only, not on the full critic which includes the classifier $p(y|x)$.

paper.title: Generalizing semi-supervised generative adversarial networks to regression using feature contrasting
paper.abstract: In this work, we generalize semi-supervised generative adversarial networks (GANs) from classification problems to regression problems. In the last few years, the importance of improving the training of neural networks using semi-supervised training has been demonstrated for classification problems. We present a novel loss function, called feature contrasting, resulting in a discriminator which can distinguish between fake and real data based on feature statistics. This method avoids potential biases and limitations of alternative approaches. The generalization of semi-supervised GANs to the regime of regression problems of opens their use to countless applications as well as providing an avenue for a deeper understanding of how GANs function. We first demonstrate the capabilities of semi-supervised regression GANs on a toy dataset which allows for a detailed understanding of how they operate in various circumstances. This toy dataset is used to provide a theoretical basis of the semi-supervised regression GAN. We then apply the semi-supervised regression GANs to a number of real-world computer vision applications: age estimation, driving steering angle prediction, and crowd counting from single images. We perform extensive tests of what accuracy can be achieved with significantly reduced annotated data. Through the combination of the theoretical example and real-world scenarios, we demonstrate how semi-supervised GANs can be generalized to regression problems.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper proposes the Semi-supervised Regression GAN (SR-GAN), which uses features from an intermediate layer of the discriminator to enable semi-supervised learning for regression problems. The key idea is "feature contrasting": the discriminator is trained to make feature statistics of labeled and unlabeled real data similar (feature matching) while making fake data features dissimilar (feature contrasting), and the generator tries to match fake features to unlabeled features. This directly uses discriminator features to improve regression performance when limited labeled data is available, demonstrated on age estimation, steering angle prediction, and crowd counting.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap specifically mentions improving "classifiers" (i.e., classification problems), while this paper addresses regression problems. The paper does not demonstrate that its feature-contrasting approach works for semi-supervised classification tasks, which is the specific problem stated in the gap. Additionally, the gap mentions features from "the discriminator or inference net" — this paper only uses discriminator features, not features from a separate inference network. The paper also does not explore whether the feature-contrasting approach could be applied to or would benefit classification tasks.
evidence_snippets: We present a novel loss function, called feature contrasting, resulting in a discriminator which can distinguish between fake and real data based on feature statistics.

The discriminator seeks to make the unlabeled examples have a similar feature distribution as the labeled examples. The discriminator also works to have fake examples have a feature distribution as divergent from the labeled examples distribution as possible.
In this work, we propose generalizing semi-supervised GANs to regression problems.
